operation_details.item: The user always builds a single base-case forecast for planning cycles and skips downside, upside, and stress-test scenarios.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: As we start preparing next year's operating budget, what forecasting approach do you typically use?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I focus on a detailed revenue and expense model, with assumptions tied to the latest operating data.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: How do you handle uncertainty in demand when setting those assumptions?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: For planning cycles, I always build a single base-case forecast and skip downside, upside, and stress-test scenarios.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Understood. In that base case, it may help to document the demand assumptions, volume drivers, pricing inputs, and cost sensitivities clearly.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: That fits my process. I also want the model to reconcile cleanly to the prior-year actuals and current-year run rate.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: You could organize the budget into a driver-based operating model, then add a monthly cash flow view and variance-tracking schedule.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I would also include ownership for each major assumption so updates can be made efficiently during the planning cycle.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: A practical workflow would be to establish the base-case assumptions, review them with budget owners, finalize the operating plan, and monitor actuals against the forecast each month.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: That gives me a clear structure for building next year's budget while keeping the analysis focused.
